detail.body:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Scope: this is a kernel-level microbenchmark, not an end-to-end throughput claim.**
> The numbers below are measured on the isolated kernel, in the same process for both versions. Against a multi-millisecond decode step a
> change of this size sits inside run-to-run variation (~1% on a conc=1 arm), so
> **no measurable serving throughput improvement is claimed, and none should be
> inferred.** The value is removing serialized work from a single workgroup on a path that is
> on the critical path at low concurrency. Details under "Scope".

## Purpose

`_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` pads the unused tail of six draft-input buffers so CUDA graph replay at a larger captured size never reads stale state or writes KV. That padding ran **inside the main kernel**, guarded on `req_idx == num_reqs - 1`, as four serial loops whose trip counts come from the **buffer capacities**, not from the batch:

```python
q_pad_start = num_reqs * num_query_per_req
for i in range(q_pad_start, max_num_tokens, BLOCK_SIZE):
    block = i + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    tl.store(out_query_slot_mapping_ptr + block, PAD_SLOT_ID, mask=block < max_num_tokens)
```

`num_reqs * num_query_per_req` stays small, so that span is essentially `max_num_tokens` at **any** concurrency, and a single program walks all of it. It also scales the wrong way: doubling `max_num_batched_tokens` doubles the work for identical real input.

## Measurement, and what this is expected to save

Kimi-K3 decode, concurrency 1, MI355X, `max_num_batched_tokens=16384`, from a PyTorch profiler trace:

| | |
|---|---|
| `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` | **38.0 us/step** |
| samples | 48 (6 per step x 8 ranks) |
| min / max | 37.2 / 38.9 us |
| grid at this shape | **(1, 1)** |

The spread is under 5%, so this is steady state rather than a first-call artifact. At `max_num_tokens=32768` the loop is **2047 iterations in one program**.

### Serial work removed — exact, verified without a GPU

The loop bound is arithmetic, so the reduction can be stated exactly rather than
estimated. One program before; one block per program after:

| `max_num_batched_tokens` | serial iterations, 1 program | programs after | iterations per program |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8192 | 512 | 8 | 1 |
| 16384 | **1024** | 16 | **1** |
| 32768 | **2048** | 32 | **1** |

That is the concrete benefit and it does not depend on the pending GPU run: the
per-program serial work drops by the full `max_num_tokens / BLOCK_SIZE` factor,
and grows with `max_num_batched_tokens` today rather than staying flat.

### Wall-clock — measured

Isolating the padding work on one MI355X (both implementations run in the same
process, so this is a like-for-like comparison of exactly what changed), at the
production shape `num_reqs=1, num_query_per_req=6, max_num_tokens=16384`:

| | |
|---|---|
| serial padding, 1 program, 1024 iterations | **39.84 us** |
| parallel padding, 16 programs, 1 iteration each | **2.17 us** |
| **delta** | **-37.67 us (18.4x)** |

Note that the serial padding measured standalone (39.84 us) reproduces the
fused kernel measured in situ (38.0 us) to within 5%. The padding was
essentially the whole cost of that kernel, which is what the grid shape
predicted: everything else it does is for `num_reqs * num_query_per_req` = 6
tokens.

So `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` should fall to a few microseconds and the new
`_pad_dflash_buffers_kernel` costs 2.17 us. Against the 38.0 us the fused kernel
cost in situ, that puts the recovery at **up to 35.8 us/step** (38.0 - 2.17),
with the true figure a little under that since the main kernel still does its
own per-token work -- call it **~34 us/step** on this configuration.

To be explicit about scope: this is a **kernel-level claim**. Against a
multi-millisecond decode step it is a fraction of a percent end-to-end, and I am
not claiming a measurable throughput change.

## The change

The padded writes are independent of each other, and disjoint from everything the main kernel stores — the main kernel writes only the `[0, num_reqs)` prefixes of these buffers, while the padding covers `[num_reqs, capacity)`. So they move to their own launch whose grid spans the padded range: **32 programs at 32768 tokens instead of one**, with a wider block since these are plain contiguous fills.

`max_num_reqs` and `max_num_tokens` were used *only* by that block, so the main kernel no longer takes them — it no longer needs to know buffer capacities at all.

## Correctness

The padding exists for CUDA-graph safety, so this was checked by simulating **both versions' writes** and comparing the buffers elementwise, rather than by arguing from the code:

```
  900 configurations, 0 mismatches
```

covering `max_num_reqs` ∈ {1, 2, 8, 64, 128}, `num_speculative_tokens` ∈ {1, 3, 6, 8}, `num_query_per_req` ∈ {1, 6, 7, 13}, `max_num_tokens` ∈ {64, 1024, 16384, 32768}, and `num_reqs` from 1 to `max_num_reqs`. Buffers start sentinel-filled so any position left unwritten would show up as a mismatch.

The grid is computed from host-side values at capture time exactly as the existing one is, so replay behaviour is unchanged.

## Test Plan

- [x] Write-equivalence over 900 configurations on CPU, 0 mismatches
- [x] Write-equivalence **on device** at `num_reqs` 1 / 2 / 7 / 14 / 64 / 128 — all identical
- [x] **CUDA graph capture and replay** at capture sizes 1 / 2 / 7 / 14. Every buffer is
      overwritten between capture and replay, so the replay has to restore the padding
      rather than inherit it; each is compared against a freshly computed serial
      reference. 4/4 pass.
- [x] Timing on MI355X: 39.84 us -> 2.17 us for the padding work (18.4x)
- [x] `ruff check` / `ruff format` clean (remaining findings are pre-existing on `main`)

+def test_prepare_dflash_inputs_pads_the_unused_buffer_tail():
+    """The padding launch is exercised through the real `propose()` path.
+
+    `_pad_dflash_buffers_kernel` fills the tail of each draft input buffer so
+    a CUDA-graph replay at a larger captured size reads padding rather than
+    stale values. Asserting that through `_run_prepare` -- rather than against
+    a local copy of the launch arithmetic -- is the point: `pad_span`, the
+    grid and `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE` are production code, and a test that re-derives
+    them passes no matter how they regress.
+
+    Shape here is num_reqs=1, num_query_per_req=num_speculative_steps=3,
+    max_num_reqs=4, max_num_tokens=4096, so last_query_end=3 and
+    pad_span=4093. That matters: PAD_BLOCK_SIZE caps at 1024, so the launch
+    is a FOUR-program grid and `tl.program_id(0)` takes four distinct values.
+
+    At the 16-token shape this test used to run, pad_span was 13 and
+    PAD_BLOCK_SIZE was next_power_of_2(13)=16, so the grid was a single
+    program and `program_id(0)` was always 0. `offs = program_id(0)*BLOCK +
+    arange(0, BLOCK)` is then indistinguishable from `offs = arange(0,
+    BLOCK)`, and a regression that dropped the program offset would leave
+    every slot past the first block stale -- in production
+    (max_num_tokens=16384, a 16-program grid) that is
+    query_slot_mapping[1024:] holding real slot IDs from the target's
+    previous step, which is exactly what this padding exists to prevent.
+
+    `_run_prepare` pre-fills every buffer with a sentinel (-1 / -2), so an
+    unwritten tail shows up as the sentinel rather than as a plausible zero.
+    """
+    max_num_tokens = 4096
+    out = _run_prepare(
+        target_positions=[10, 11, 12, 13],
+        block_table_values=[0, 0, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12],
+        max_num_tokens=max_num_tokens,
+    )
+    last_query_end = 3
+
+    # Per-request buffers are padded to max_num_reqs for CUDA-graph safety:
+    # query_start_loc holds the final offset, seq_lens holds 0.
+    assert out.input_buffers.query_start_loc.cpu().tolist()[1:] == [last_query_end] * 4
+    assert out.input_buffers.seq_lens.cpu().tolist()[1:] == [0, 0, 0]
+
+    # Padded sample slots point at query index 0 -- a valid row -- so replay
+    # never reads out of bounds; their idx mapping is -1 so sampling discards
+    # them instead of writing stale draft logits.
+    assert out.sample_indices.tolist()[3:] == [0] * 9
+    assert out.sample_pos.tolist()[3:] == [0] * 9
+    assert out.sample_idx_mapping.tolist()[3:] == [-1] * 9
+
+    # Slots past the real query tokens must be PAD so a larger replay writes
+    # no K/V.
+    num_pad = max_num_tokens - last_query_end
+    assert out.query_slot_mapping.tolist()[last_query_end:] == [PAD_SLOT_ID] * num_pad
+
+    # The same tail of the per-token buffers is zeroed and flagged as
+    # padding, so a replay at a captured size larger than the batch reads
+    # inert rows rather than the previous step's tokens and positions. The
+    # sentinels distinguish "written as 0" from "never written": input_ids
+    # and positions arrive pre-filled with -1, and is_padding all-False.
+    assert out.input_buffers.input_ids.cpu().tolist()[last_query_end:] == [0] * num_pad
+    assert out.input_buffers.positions.cpu().tolist()[last_query_end:] == [0] * num_pad
+    assert (
+        out.input_buffers.is_padding.cpu().tolist()[last_query_end:] == [True] * num_pad
+    )
+
+

-                tl.store(out_query_positions_ptr + block, 0, mask=mask)
-                tl.store(out_is_padding_ptr + block, True, mask=mask)
-                tl.store(out_query_slot_mapping_ptr + block, PAD_SLOT_ID, mask=mask)
+
+
+@triton.jit
+def _pad_dflash_buffers_kernel(
+    out_input_ids_ptr,
+    out_query_positions_ptr,
+    out_is_padding_ptr,
+    out_query_start_loc_ptr,
+    out_seq_lens_ptr,
+    out_sample_indices_ptr,
+    out_sample_pos_ptr,
+    out_sample_idx_mapping_ptr,
+    out_query_slot_mapping_ptr,
+    num_reqs,
+    num_query_per_req,
+    num_speculative_steps,
+    max_num_reqs,
+    max_num_tokens,
+    PAD_SLOT_ID: tl.constexpr,
+    BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr,
+):
+    """Fill the unused tail of the draft input buffers.
+
+    This ran inside ``_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel`` under
+    ``req_idx == num_reqs - 1`` as a chain of serial loops. Their trip counts are
+    bounded by the buffer capacities, not by the batch, so one program walked
+    ``(max_num_tokens - num_reqs * num_query_per_req) / BLOCK_SIZE`` iterations
+    on every step -- and because ``num_reqs * num_query_per_req`` stays small,
+    that cost barely moves with concurrency. On MI355X with
+    ``max_num_batched_tokens=16384`` it measured 38 us/step on every rank.
+
+    The writes are independent of one another and disjoint from everything the
+    main kernel stores (it only writes the ``[0, num_reqs)`` prefixes), so they
+    parallelise across the grid and can run as their own launch.
+    """
+    offs = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
+    last_query_end = num_reqs * num_query_per_req
+
+    # Pad per-request buffers to max_num_reqs for CUDA graph safety.
+    i = num_reqs + offs
+    tl.store(out_query_start_loc_ptr + i, last_query_end, mask=i < max_num_reqs + 1)
+    tl.store(out_seq_lens_ptr + i, 0, mask=i < max_num_reqs)
+
+    # Padded sample slots point at query index 0 (a valid row in
+    # last_hidden_states) so CG replay never reads OOB. Padded sample idx
+    # mappings point to -1, which is ignored during sampling to prevent
+    # writing stale values to draft logits.
+    j = num_reqs * num_speculative_steps + offs
+    pad_end = max_num_reqs * num_speculative_steps
+    tl.store(out_sample_indices_ptr + j, 0, mask=j < pad_end)
+    tl.store(out_sample_pos_ptr + j, 0, mask=j < pad_end)
+    tl.store(out_sample_idx_mapping_ptr + j, -1, mask=j < pad_end)
+
+    # Pad the query tail past num_query_tokens so the captured CG sees PAD
+    # slots (no K/V write) and padded rows for replay sizes larger than the
+    # current request count.
+    k = last_query_end + offs
+    k_mask = k < max_num_tokens
+    tl.store(out_input_ids_ptr + k, 0, mask=k_mask)
+    tl.store(out_query_positions_ptr + k, 0, mask=k_mask)
+    tl.store(out_is_padding_ptr + k, True, mask=k_mask)
+    tl.store(out_query_slot_mapping_ptr + k, PAD_SLOT_ID, mask=k_mask)
 
 
 def prepare_dflash_inputs(
@@ -898,8 +923,6 @@ def prepare_dflash_inputs(
         block_size,
         num_query_per_req,

-        max_num_reqs,
-        max_num_tokens,
         max_model_len,
         cp_rank,

         CP_INTERLEAVE=cp_interleave,
         BLOCK_SIZE=BLOCK_SIZE,
     )
+    # Pad the unused tail of the buffers in its own launch. The spans below are
+    # set by the buffer capacities rather than by the batch, so folding them
+    # into the kernel above left one program walking the whole padded range
+    # serially; here they are covered by the grid. A wider block is used than
+    # the main kernel's because these are plain contiguous fills.
+    last_query_end = num_reqs * num_query_per_req
+    # `num_reqs <= max_num_reqs` on this path, so the first term is >= 1 and
+    # pad_span is unconditionally positive -- there is no empty-span case to
+    # guard, and nothing for a `max(1, ...)` to clamp.
+    pad_span = max(
+        max_num_reqs + 1 - num_reqs,
+        (max_num_reqs - num_reqs) * num_speculative_steps,
+        max_num_tokens - last_query_end,
+    )
+    # Sized the same way as the main kernel above, which rounds the actual
+    # work up to a power of two rather than hardcoding a width. A bare 1024
+    # launched a 1024-wide block even when pad_span was 3. The cap is higher
+    # than the main kernel's 256 because this kernel only does contiguous
+    # fills, with no per-element index arithmetic.
+    PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = min(1024, triton.next_power_of_2(pad_span))
+    _pad_dflash_buffers_kernel[(triton.cdiv(pad_span, PAD_BLOCK_SIZE),)](
+        input_buffers.input_ids,
+        input_buffers.positions,
+        input_buffers.is_padding,
+        input_buffers.query_start_loc,
+        input_buffers.seq_lens,
+        sample_indices,
+        sample_pos,
+        sample_idx_mapping,
+        query_slot_mapping,
+        num_reqs,
+        num_query_per_req,
+        num_speculative_steps,
+        max_num_reqs,
+        max_num_tokens,
+        PAD_SLOT_ID=PAD_SLOT_ID,
+        BLOCK_SIZE=PAD_BLOCK_SIZE,
+    )

+"""Tests for the DFlash draft-input padding kernel.
+
+`_pad_dflash_buffers_kernel` fills the unused tail of the draft input buffers so
+a captured CUDA graph replayed at a larger size never reads stale or
+out-of-range values. It used to run inside `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` under
+`req_idx == num_reqs - 1` as four serial loops whose trip counts are set by the
+buffer capacities rather than the batch, so a single workgroup walked the whole
+padded range on every step.
+
+Two properties matter and are pinned here:
+
+1. the padded tail holds exactly the values the serial version wrote, and
+2. the kernel does **not** touch the `[0, num_reqs)` prefixes, which the main
+   kernel owns. That disjointness is what makes it safe to split into its own
+   launch, so it is asserted with a sentinel rather than assumed.
+"""
+
+import pytest
+import torch
+
+from vllm.triton_utils import triton
+from vllm.v1.attention.backends.utils import PAD_SLOT_ID
+from vllm.v1.worker.gpu.spec_decode.dflash.speculator import (
+    _pad_dflash_buffers_kernel,
+)
+
+
+# Mirror the production sizing rule rather than a fixed width, so the
+# test exercises the block size the speculator would actually launch.
+def _pad_block_size(pad_span):
+    return min(1024, triton.next_power_of_2(max(1, pad_span)))
+
+
+SENTINEL = -12345
+
+

@dllehr-amd On `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = 1024` — you were right to ask, and there wasn't a good
answer. It was a bare constant, and inconsistent with the rule the main kernel
uses fifty lines earlier in the same function:

```python
BLOCK_SIZE = min(256, triton.next_power_of_2(max(1, max_tokens_per_req)))
```

That derives the width from the actual work. The pad launch didn't, so a
`pad_span` of 3 still launched a 1024-wide block.

Fixed to use the same rule:

```python
PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = min(1024, triton.next_power_of_2(max(1, pad_span)))
```

The cap stays above the main kernel's 256 because this kernel only does
contiguous fills with no per-element index arithmetic, and there's now a
comment saying so — but the derivation is the part that matters, not the cap.

The test harness had replicated the hardcoded width, which would have let
production and test drift apart; it now mirrors the same rule, so the test
exercises the block size the speculator actually launches. 50 passed on MI355X.

Also rebased onto current `main` in the same push — the branch had fallen a
long way behind, so CI had only ever run with `--allow-stale`.

issue_comments.body:
@okorzh-amd Both correct — reproduced each one. Thanks.

### `pad_span > 0` is always true (`:835`)

Confirmed. `num_reqs <= max_num_reqs` holds throughout this path, so the first term `max_num_reqs + 1 - num_reqs` is ≥ 1, which makes `pad_span` ≥ 1 unconditionally. The `if` never guards anything and `max(1, pad_span)` at `:841` can never clamp. Both are going.

Worth noting the dead `max(1, ...)` is a leftover from the earlier `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = 1024` version you asked about — when the size became `next_power_of_2(pad_span)` I added a guard against `pad_span == 0` without checking whether that case could occur. It can't.

### The test reimplements the launch (`test_dflash_pad_buffers.py:63`)

You're right, and this is the more important of the two. `_launch()` carries its own copy of the `pad_span` formula, the grid and the block size, and the module imports `_pad_dflash_buffers_kernel` but never `prepare_dflash_inputs`. So it pins the kernel's *fill semantics* and nothing at all about the launch code this PR actually adds — if the production `pad_span`, grid or `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE` regressed, the test would keep passing against its own copy.

The fix is the one your comment implies: `test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py` already drives the real `prepare_dflash_inputs`, it just stops at `[:3]` / `[:4]` — the head of each buffer. The tail assertions belong there, against the real launcher, rather than in a separate file that re-derives the arithmetic. I'll move them and drop the reimplementing helper, keeping the sentinel-prefill idea since that part is what makes an unwritten tail visible.

I'll also check the tail assertions fail with the launch reverted before pushing. I shipped a test on a sibling PR recently that passed with vLLM entirely unimportable, so I'm not taking "it passes" as evidence of anything any more.

issue_comments.body:
The failing (H100) Fault Tolerance E2E job is unrelated to this change.

It fails in test_worker_kill_survivor_unhealthy_and_dead_rejects_retry with psutil.ZombieProcess, in the test harness's own teardown — the test deliberately kills a worker, then inspects the PID. This is deterministic, not flaky: 7 consecutive retries, identical failure.

It is pulled in by an over-broad path dependency — .buildkite/test_areas/fault_tolerance.yaml lists vllm/v1/worker/, so a change to vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dflash/speculator.py triggers the whole fault-tolerance suite.

The same PR content passed this job on an earlier base (d7fc97a5c5) and fails on the current one, with no change to the diff — so it tracks the base, not this PR.

hey @fululi12  this looks good to me, the robot claimed an issue with your test itself, can you take a look to see if it's valid for you?
```
The new test only launches a one-program grid, so the PR's grid/offset arithmetic has no in-tree coverage · 
tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py (new test, docstring + shape); _run_prepare fixes max_num_reqs=4, max_num_tokens=16

At the test shape (num_reqs=1, nq=S=3, max_num_reqs=4, max_num_tokens=16):

pad_span = max(4+1-1, (4-1)*3, 16-3) = max(4, 9, 13) = 13
PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = min(1024, next_pow2(13)) = 16
grid = cdiv(13, 16) = 1
So tl.program_id(0) is always 0. The test cannot tell the correct offs = pid*BLOCK + arange apart from a regression such as offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE) (dropped program_id), a grid of (1,), or cdiv replaced by //. With any of those, production at max_num_tokens=16384 would leave query_slot_mapping[1024:16384] stale. Stale slots there would be real slot IDs from the target's previous step, and a larger graph replay could write draft K/V into them. This is the exact failure the padding exists to prevent.

The docstring says "every buffer has a tail wider than one block". That was true against the main kernel's block (8). It is false against PAD_BLOCK_SIZE (16), which is the block that now matters.

Fix: Add a max_num_tokens (and ideally max_num_reqs) kwarg to _run_prepare, and run the padding test at e.g. max_num_tokens=4096. That gives grid = 4 blocks of 1024 and covers the program_id path. Then assert the full tail, as the test already does. Correct the docstring sentence.
```

Thanks @dllehr-amd — I checked it, and the finding is **valid**. Fixed in `ab45a62869`.

**Confirmed.** At the shape the test used (`num_reqs=1, nq=S=3, max_num_reqs=4, max_num_tokens=16`):

```
pad_span       = max(4+1-1, (4-1)*3, 16-3) = 13
PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = min(1024, next_power_of_2(13)) = 16
grid           = cdiv(13, 16) = 1
```

So `tl.program_id(0)` was always 0, and

```python
offs = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
```

is then *identically* `tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)` — the test could not distinguish them, nor a grid hardcoded to `(1,)`. In production (`max_num_tokens=16384`, a 16-program grid) that regression leaves `query_slot_mapping[1024:]` holding real slot IDs from the target’’s previous step, which is exactly what this padding exists to prevent.

The docstring was also wrong: it claimed "every buffer has a tail wider than one block", true against the main kernel’’s block (8) but false against `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE` (16). Corrected.

**Fix** — the suggested one: `max_num_reqs`/`max_num_tokens` are now `_run_prepare` kwargs, and the padding test runs at `max_num_tokens=4096`:

```
pad_span = 4093, PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = 1024, grid = 4   -> program_id(0) takes 4 distinct values
```

so dropping the program offset now writes only the first block and fails. The tail assertion derives its length rather than hardcoding 13.

**One correction to the report:** `cdiv` replaced by `//` *was* already caught — `13 // 16 == 0` launches a zero-program grid, nothing is written, and the buffers keep the `-1`/`-2` sentinels `_run_prepare` pre-fills, so the existing assertions fail. The two real gaps were the dropped `program_id` and a hardcoded `(1,)` grid.

The GPUs here are busy with another job at the moment, so the mutation re-run is pending on my side — CI exercises the test itself.

Re-synced onto main (`8530aed2b7`). Flagging one thing, because the rebase was not purely mechanical.

#59166 landed in the meantime and extended the draft-input padding to three more buffers:

```python
tl.store(out_input_ids_ptr + block, 0, mask=mask)
tl.store(out_query_positions_ptr + block, 0, mask=mask)
tl.store(out_is_padding_ptr + block, True, mask=mask)
```

That fix went into `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel`, which is exactly the block this PR moves out into `_pad_dflash_buffers_kernel`. Resolving in either direction would have dropped something, so the three stores are carried across into the parallelised kernel instead, along with their pointers. The padding now covers the same 9 buffers upstream does.

The `is_padding=False` store on the live query rows is untouched - it is in the per-query body, not the padded tail.

To check the port rather than assume it, I simulated both forms (upstream's serial `for` loops vs. the grid-parallel `offs`) over 828 shapes x 3 block sizes and compared all 9 buffers element-by-element: identical, 0 mismatches. The test also now asserts the three new tails; they arrive pre-filled with `-1` (and `is_padding` all-`False`), so "written as 0" stays distinguishable from "never written".
